title: Mini Command Parser
story: You're building a REPL (Read-Eval-Print Loop) for a developer tool. Users type commands like 'SAY hello', 'ADD 5 3', or 'RANDOM 1 10'. Each command has its own arguments and its own way of failing. Your parser needs to split the input, identify the command, parse arguments, and return either the result string or a helpful error.
why: Building a multi-command parser teaches string splitting, command dispatch, argument parsing, and error propagation — the exact pattern behind every CLI tool, chatbot, and game console.
analogy: A command parser is like a restaurant kitchen's order system. The waiter writes 'BURGER medium fries' on a ticket (the command string). The kitchen reads the first word to know which station to send it to (command dispatch). The grill station reads 'medium' and 'fries' as arguments and starts cooking. If the ticket says 'PIZZA' — the kitchen doesn't have a pizza station, so they send back 'Unknown command' rather than guessing.
try_it: Add UPPER and LOWER commands that convert the argument to uppercase/lowercase using string.str_upper and string.str_lower. Add a LEN command that returns the length of the argument. Add a REPEAT command: 'REPEAT hello 3' prints 'hellohellohello'. Add error handling for REPEAT when the count isn't a number or is negative. What if someone types 'ADD 5' with only one number?
tips: Split on the FIRST space only — the rest is the argument string (commands can have multi-word arguments)
Use `?` inside handler functions to propagate parse errors up to the main parser
Each command handler is self-contained: it knows what arguments it needs and how to validate them
common_mistakes: Splitting on ALL spaces — 'SAY hello world' should split into cmd='SAY', args='hello world', not three parts
Using `?` before checking if enough arguments exist — if there's no space, str_to_int on empty string will give a confusing error
Forgetting that `math.random_range` might not exist if not imported — always verify stdlib functions are available
